Vignette:
# Clinical Vignette: Vinh

Vinh was twenty-eight when the police stopped him outside a convenience store on a Friday evening in late August. He had stepped out for cigarettes while his wife, Lan, waited in their car three blocks away. Two officers approached him from behind as he stood at the counter. He did not hear them call out. When he felt a hand grip his shoulder, he turned—a reflex—and one of the officers interpreted the movement as resistance. What followed was a blur of force: his arm wrenched behind his back, his face pressed against the cold counter, his own voice shouting that he had done nothing, that this was a mistake. The officers were looking for someone matching his general description in connection with a robbery two blocks away. Vinh was released after forty minutes when store footage cleared him, but the damage was already done. He had been slammed against a hard surface, restrained, accused of a crime he did not commit, and left with the knowledge that his body could be treated that way by people with authority and that no amount of innocence would have stopped it.

In the weeks that followed, Vinh found himself unable to enter rooms the way he used to. He would position himself with his back to the wall—at the dinner table, in the living room while watching television, even in the bathroom mirror. Lan noticed first. She would ask him to sit beside her on the couch, and he would shift to the armchair, his back firmly against wood. When she asked why, he said nothing at first. Later, he said he just felt better that way. What he did not tell her was that the moment his back was exposed—when he sat facing outward into a room—his chest would tighten and his eyes would dart to the doorway, the window, anywhere someone could enter unseen. He had come to believe that if he could see the whole room, see everyone in it, see where danger might come from, then perhaps it would not happen again. The violation had taught him that the world was not arranged for his safety, and his body had learned to live as though he were always about to be approached from behind.

The rumination began almost immediately. Vinh would replay the moment of the grip on his shoulder for hours, sometimes lying awake next to Lan, sometimes during work. He blamed himself relentlessly—he should have heard them, should have turned more slowly, should have anticipated that his appearance might trigger suspicion. If he had simply waited until morning to buy cigarettes, if he had gone to the store two blocks away instead, if he had turned around differently. The self-blame felt like a kind of control: if this had been his fault, then he could prevent it next time by being more careful, more aware, more compliant. But the rumination never resolved; it only deepened, circling back to the same moment, the same impossible choices.

Within two months, Vinh began using crystal methamphetamine. A coworker offered it to him one afternoon, and he took it because it quieted the loop in his head. The drug gave him a few hours where he was not replaying the counter, not blaming himself, not vigilant. Lan did not know at first. She knew only that he was irritable, that he was sleeping less, that he had stopped going out except for work. When she tried to talk to him about what had happened, about whether he wanted to see someone, he would leave the room. Thinking about the event felt unbearable—as though naming it, describing it, would make it more real, more solid in his mind. It was easier to avoid the thought entirely, to fill the space with work and, increasingly, with the drug that made the avoidance possible.

His carpentry suffered. Vinh had been reliable for eight years, but now he was missing days or arriving late, his hands shaky, his concentration fractured. His foreman pulled him aside in November and asked directly if he was using. Vinh denied it, but the work dried up. Fewer calls, fewer jobs. Lan found a pipe in his jacket pocket in January and confronted him. She wept. He wept. He said he would stop, and he tried, but the moment he stopped using, the rumination returned with such force that he could not sit still. He would pace the apartment, his back never fully to the wall, his mind never fully at rest.

What frightened him most was the possibility that something bad would happen while he was distracted, while his guard was down. When Lan was late coming home from work, he assumed an accident had occurred. When a contractor job took longer than expected, he was certain something had gone wrong, that someone was hurt, that he should have anticipated the delay and prevented whatever disaster was unfolding. He could not relax even when Lan was beside him, even when the apartment was locked and quiet. His body was always half-tensed, always ready.

It was Lan who finally insisted he see someone. She gave him the name of a therapist and said she could not watch him disappear anymore. Vinh called the clinic three weeks later, sitting in his truck in a parking lot, his back against the door so he could see the whole windshield. He told the intake worker that he did not know if therapy would help, that he was not sure he could talk about what happened without falling apart. What he was most hoping for, though he barely admitted it to himself, was to sit beside his wife on the couch again without his body screaming that danger was imminent—to feel, for once, that his back was safe.
